blocks.p: A **square matrix** has the same number of rows and columns, $n \times n$. Only square matrices have a determinant, an inverse, a **main diagonal** (the entries $a_{11}, a_{22}, \ldots, a_{nn}$) and a **trace** (the sum of that diagonal).

$A^2$ means $A \times A$ using matrix multiplication (each entry is a row of $A$ times a column of $A$), not squaring each entry. It's only defined for square matrices, since the number of columns of the first factor must match the rows of the second.
Squaring each entry instead would give $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 9 & 16 \end{bmatrix}$, which is a different (and wrong) answer.
Multiplying every entry of an $n \times n$ matrix by a constant $k$ scales the determinant by $k^n$, not just $k$:
If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $|A|=5$, then $|2A| = 2^3(5) = 40$.

blocks.p: For a matrix equation $AX=B$ with square matrix $A$:

list: If $|A| \neq 0$, the system has exactly one solution, $X = A^{-1}B$.
If $|A|=0$ (A is singular) and $(\text{adj }A)B \ne O$, the system has **no solution** at all: it's inconsistent.
If $|A| = 0$ and $(\text{adj }A)B = O$, the test doesn't decide. The system may have infinitely many solutions or none, so it has to be checked directly, for example by elimination.
**Squaring each entry.** $A^2$ is $A$ multiplied by itself as matrices, as the example above shows.
**Writing $|kA| = k|A|$.** Each of the $n$ rows picks up a factor of $k$, so it's $k^n|A|$.
**Assuming $AB = BA$.** Matrix multiplication isn't commutative, so $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$, not $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$.
**Treating $(\text{adj }A)B = O$ as "infinitely many solutions".** With $|A| = 0$ it can also mean no solution.

exam.note: Determinants of square matrices and the adjoint and inverse are listed in the matrices units of the JEE Main 2026 and JEE Advanced 2026 syllabi and the 2025-26 CBSE Class XII syllabus. JEE Main and CBSE also name the consistency of a system of linear equations, and JEE Advanced its solution.

related.intro: Whether a matrix is singular is exactly what decides whether a system of equations solved by the matrix method has a unique solution in the first place.
